title: Water, impurities and hardness
learn: Natural water contains dissolved and suspended impurities; hardness is chiefly associated with dissolved calcium and magnesium salts.
Temporary (carbonate) hardness is associated mainly with bicarbonates; permanent (non-carbonate) hardness is associated mainly with chlorides and sulphates.
Hardness is conventionally expressed as CaCO₃ equivalent so salts with different formula masses can be compared on one common basis.

sections.heading: Introduction and impurities in natural water
paragraphs: The textbook treats water as naturally impure. Rain water, river water, lake water, spring water and well water acquire impurities from the atmosphere, soil, rocks and biological surroundings.
The impurities discussed include suspended matter, dissolved salts and gases, and biological matter. For hardness calculations, the dissolved salts of calcium and magnesium are the most important.

book_refs.note: Introduction, sources and impurities of water

sections.heading: Hardness of water
paragraphs: Hardness is the characteristic of water by which it does not readily form lather with soap. The textbook attributes hardness mainly to dissolved salts of calcium and magnesium.

Temporary hardness, also called carbonate hardness, is caused principally by bicarbonates of calcium and magnesium and can be removed by boiling. Permanent hardness, also called non-carbonate hardness, is caused principally by chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium and is not removed by boiling.
bullets: Permanent hardness: chiefly chlorides and sulphates such as \(\mathrm{CaCl_2}\), \(\mathrm{MgCl_2}\), \(\mathrm{CaSO_4}\) and \(\mathrm{MgSO_4}\).

sections.heading: Removal of temporary hardness by boiling
paragraphs: On boiling, bicarbonates decompose and form insoluble precipitates, thereby removing temporary hardness.

sections.heading: CaCO₃ equivalents
paragraphs: Hardness-producing substances are converted to their calcium-carbonate equivalents. The textbook uses the equivalent mass of \(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\), namely 50, as the common reference.
formulas: \(\text{CaCO}_3\text{ equivalent}=\dfrac{\text{mass of hardness-producing substance}\times 50}{\text{chemical equivalent of hardness-producing substance}}\)

tables.caption: Selected CaCO₃ conversion factors from textbook Table 1

sections.heading: Units and degree of hardness
paragraphs: The textbook defines hardness in parts per million (ppm), milligrams per litre (mg/L), Clark's degree, French degree and milliequivalents per litre. For dilute aqueous solutions, 1 mg/L as CaCO₃ is numerically equal to 1 ppm.

self_checks.question: Why is hardness expressed as CaCO₃ equivalent?
self_checks.answer: It converts different hardness-producing salts to one common basis, making their contributions directly additive and comparable.

self_checks.question: Which type of hardness is removed by boiling?

title: Hardness calculations and complexometric estimation
learn: Hardness calculations first convert every hardness-producing constituent to its CaCO₃ equivalent and then add the contributions.
EDTA forms stable soluble complexes with metal ions such as Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺.
With Eriochrome Black T at about pH 10, the metal–indicator complex is wine red; at the EDTA end point the liberated indicator gives a blue colour.

sections.heading: Numerical method for hardness
paragraphs: For a water analysis reported in mg/L, multiply the concentration of each hardness-producing salt by its CaCO₃ conversion factor and add the resulting CaCO₃-equivalent concentrations. Separate temporary and permanent contributors when the question asks for both.

sections.heading: Worked example — hardness from dissolved salts
paragraphs: A water sample contains \(\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}=73\,mg/L\), \(\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}=162\,mg/L\), \(\mathrm{MgCl_2}=95\,mg/L\) and \(\mathrm{CaSO_4}=136\,mg/L\).
Temporary hardness: \(73\times\dfrac{100}{146}+162\times\dfrac{100}{162}=50+100=150\,ppm\).
Permanent hardness: \(95\times\dfrac{100}{95}+136\times\dfrac{100}{136}=100+100=200\,ppm\).
Total hardness: \(150+200=350\,ppm\).
**Final answer:** Temporary hardness \(=150\,ppm\), permanent hardness \(=200\,ppm\), total hardness \(=350\,ppm\).

sections.heading: Complexometric method using EDTA
paragraphs: The textbook describes EDTA as a complexometric reagent that forms chelate complexes with metal ions. In alkaline medium, EDTA reacts with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ to form stable soluble metal–EDTA complexes.

Eriochrome Black T (EBT) is used at about pH 10. Before the end point, the metal–indicator complex is wine red. As EDTA binds the metal ions, EBT is released; the end point is the change from wine red to blue.

tables.caption: Relevant complexometric indicator information from the supplied appendix

sections.heading: Source boundary for the R25 water-hardness titration
paragraphs: The supplied textbook pages support the EDTA complexation principle, EBT indicator, pH and colour change. They do not present a single standalone water-hardness-by-EDTA laboratory procedure in the same form as the R25 wording. A water-hardness-specific procedure should therefore be added only from an approved source or class/lab material.

cautions: R25's exact water-hardness EDTA procedure is not fully stated in the supplied textbook pages.

What is the first step in a hardness numerical when salts are given in mg/L?

title: Boiler troubles: scales and sludges
learn: Scale is a hard, adherent deposit on boiler surfaces; sludge is a soft, loose, non-adherent deposit.
Scale lowers heat transfer, wastes fuel, lowers boiler safety and efficiency, and can contribute to dangerous overheating.
R25 requires scales and sludges, not the chapter's later boiler-corrosion topics.

sections.heading: Scale and sludge formation
paragraphs: When dissolved salts are concentrated by evaporation in a boiler, some precipitate. A soft, loose and slimy precipitate is called sludge; a hard, adherent deposit on the inner wall is called scale.

figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 1, Scale and sludge in boilers, on textbook page 7.

sections.heading: Causes of scale formation
bullets: Deposition of calcium sulphate as its solubility decreases at high temperature.
Silica may form hard silicate deposits such as calcium or magnesium silicate.

sections.heading: Disadvantages of scale
paragraphs: Because scale has low thermal conductivity, more fuel is needed to transfer the same amount of heat. The textbook also lists reduced boiler safety, reduced efficiency and danger of explosion when thick scale causes severe local overheating.

tables.caption: Textbook table: effect of scale thickness on fuel wastage

sections.heading: Prevention by water treatment
paragraphs: The textbook separates prevention into external softening before boiler use and internal treatment within the boiler. R25 names three internal methods: colloidal, phosphate and Calgon conditioning.

book_refs.note: Boiler scale, sludge, causes and effects

self_checks.question: What is the main physical difference between scale and sludge?
self_checks.answer: Scale is hard and adherent; sludge is soft, loose and non-adherent.

title: Internal treatment of boiler feed water
learn: Colloidal conditioning converts scale-forming matter into loose non-sticky deposits.
Phosphate conditioning precipitates calcium and magnesium as removable phosphate sludge.
Calgon conditioning holds hardness ions in soluble complex form and prevents scale/sludge deposition.

sections.heading: Colloidal conditioning
paragraphs: For low-pressure boilers, the textbook describes adding organic substances such as kerosene, tannin or agar-agar. They coat scale-forming precipitates and produce non-sticky, loose deposits that can be removed by blow-down.

sections.heading: Phosphate conditioning
paragraphs: For high-pressure boilers, sodium phosphate is added so hardness salts form soft, non-adherent calcium and magnesium phosphate sludge removable by blow-down.
bullets: The textbook lists \(\mathrm{NaH_2PO_4}\), \(\mathrm{Na_2HPO_4}\) and \(\mathrm{Na_3PO_4}\); the choice depends on feed-water alkalinity.

sections.heading: Calgon conditioning
paragraphs: Calgon is sodium hexametaphosphate, represented in the textbook as \(\mathrm{(NaPO_3)_6}\). It prevents scale and sludge by forming soluble complex species with calcium salts.

book_refs.note: Internal treatment methods required by R25

self_checks.question: Which internal treatment uses sodium hexametaphosphate?

title: External treatment: ion-exchange demineralisation
learn: Ion-exchange treatment uses a cation exchanger followed by an anion exchanger.
The cation exchanger replaces dissolved cations with H⁺; the anion exchanger replaces dissolved anions with OH⁻.
The released H⁺ and OH⁻ combine to form water, giving deionised/demineralised water.

sections.heading: Cation-exchange resin
paragraphs: The textbook describes acidic cation-exchange resins carrying groups such as sulphonic acid. When hard water passes through the cation exchanger, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ and other cations are retained and equivalent H⁺ ions are released.

figures.figure_name: Acidic or cation exchange resin (sulphonate form)
figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 6, Acidic or cation exchange resin (sulphonate form), on textbook page 17.

sections.heading: Anion-exchange resin
paragraphs: The anion exchanger contains basic functional groups and releases OH⁻ in exchange for anions such as chloride and sulphate.

figures.figure_name: Basic or anion exchange resin (hydroxide form)
figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 7, Basic or anion exchange resin (hydroxide form), on textbook page 18.

sections.heading: Demineralisation unit and regeneration
paragraphs: A demineralisation plant passes water through cation and anion exchangers in sequence. The exhausted cation exchanger is regenerated with dilute acid; the exhausted anion exchanger is regenerated with dilute alkali.

figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 8, Demineralisation of water, on textbook page 19.
Placeholder for textbook Fig. 9, Regeneration of mixed-bed ion exchanger, on textbook page 20.

self_checks.question: What ions are released by the cation and anion exchangers?
self_checks.answer: The cation exchanger releases H⁺; the anion exchanger releases OH⁻.

title: Potable water and municipal treatment
learn: Potable water is water safe for drinking.
The textbook sequence is removal of suspended impurities, sedimentation/coagulation, filtration, and removal of microorganisms.
Chlorination is the R25-required disinfection method, with break-point chlorination explicitly required.

sections.heading: Potable-water specifications in the supplied textbook
paragraphs: The textbook describes drinking water as clear and odourless, pleasant in taste, cool, and free from objectionable dissolved gases and harmful disease-producing microorganisms. It also states numerical limits for hardness, chlorides, fluorides and dissolved solids.

R25 specifically labels the specifications as WHO specifications. The supplied textbook page does not identify its list as a WHO table, so this page preserves the textbook specifications but does not relabel them as WHO values.

sections.heading: Screening, sedimentation and coagulation
paragraphs: Screening removes larger suspended matter. Sedimentation allows heavier suspended particles to settle. When fine colloidal matter does not settle readily, coagulation is used to convert it into larger flocs that can settle.

sections.heading: Filtration
paragraphs: Filtration removes much of the remaining suspended matter and microorganisms by passing water through filter media. The textbook illustrates a sand filter.

figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 10, Sand filter, on textbook page 21.

sections.heading: Disinfection by chlorination
paragraphs: Chlorination is described as a widely used disinfection method. Chlorine in water forms hypochlorous acid, and the textbook attributes the disinfecting action mainly to hypochlorous acid.

figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 11, Chlorinator, on textbook page 23.

sections.heading: Break-point chlorination
paragraphs: When chlorine is added to water containing reducing substances and ammonia, the initial dose is consumed. As dosage increases, chloramines form and are then destroyed. Beyond the minimum residual point — the break point — further chlorine produces a free residual chlorine concentration. The textbook recommends dosage beyond the break point to provide effective disinfection.

figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 12, Break-point chlorination curve, on textbook page 24.

sections.heading: Overall municipal treatment flow
paragraphs: The textbook summarises municipal-water treatment in a flow diagram. The figure placeholder is retained here for the later image pass.

self_checks.question: What is break-point chlorination?
self_checks.answer: It is the stage at which chlorine demand has been satisfied and further chlorine addition begins to produce a free residual chlorine concentration.

title: Membrane separation and reverse osmosis
learn: R25 explicitly requires MF, UF and NF membrane types, their advantages and applications.
The supplied Jain & Jain pages do not contain those MF/UF/NF subsections.
The textbook does directly cover reverse osmosis for desalination of brackish or saline water.

sections.heading: R25 membrane-separation source gap
paragraphs: R25 requires Microfiltration (MF), Ultrafiltration (UF) and Nanofiltration (NF), together with their advantages and applications. These topics were not found in the supplied Unit-I textbook pages. No outside explanation has been inserted here without an approved source.

sections.heading: Reverse osmosis
paragraphs: The textbook describes reverse osmosis as a desalination method in which pressure greater than the osmotic pressure is applied on the concentrated/saline side of a semipermeable membrane. Water is thereby forced through the membrane in the reverse direction to normal osmosis, while dissolved salts are largely retained.
The textbook lists advantages including comparatively low energy demand, continuous operation, compact equipment, low operating cost and high reliability.

figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 17, Reverse osmosis cell, on textbook page 27.

cautions: MF, UF and NF remain an explicit source gap until an approved source is supplied.

self_checks.question: What pressure condition is required for reverse osmosis?
self_checks.answer: An applied pressure greater than the osmotic pressure on the concentrated/saline side.
